identity.module: Module 1 — The Business Before the Controls

purpose.whyExists: An enterprise creates value by running repeatable business processes. Risk, controls, and audit all attach to specific points in a process, so a learner cannot understand a control until they can see the process it sits inside.
purpose.whyLearnerNeeds: Auditors test controls within processes (Procure-to-Pay, Order-to-Cash). Without a mental model of how a transaction flows from start to finish, control testing is just box-ticking.
purpose.businessProblem: When people don't understand the end-to-end process, controls are placed at the wrong step, risks between handoffs go unnoticed, and audit findings miss the real exposure.

outcomes.statement: Define a business process in terms of inputs, activities, outputs, and a process owner.
Trace a simple transaction end-to-end through a named process such as Procure-to-Pay.
Locate at least two control points within a process and explain what could go wrong at each.
Explain why segregation of duties matters at process handoffs.

businessContext.note: Process thinking spans departments — a single Procure-to-Pay flow crosses Procurement, Operations, and Finance, which is exactly why handoffs are risky.

enterpriseContext.whereItLives: The operational layer of the enterprise — the repeatable flows that turn inputs into delivered value and recorded transactions.
enterpriseContext.owner: The process owner (a business leader, e.g. the Head of Procurement for P2P)
enterpriseContext.maintainer: Operations staff and the IT teams running the systems that execute the process
enterpriseContext.auditor: Internal Audit (process and control walkthroughs) and external auditors for financially significant processes

likelyQuestions: Walk me through the Procure-to-Pay process.
Where in a process would you place a control and why?
What is a process owner and why does it matter for audit?
traps: Describing software screens instead of the business flow.
Forgetting handoffs between departments, where most risk lives.
strongAnswerTraits: Describes inputs/activities/outputs and a clear owner
Connects a control to a specific step
weakAnswerTraits: Lists system features, not business steps
No notion of who owns the process
followUps: What could go wrong between approval and payment?
How would you test that the approval step actually happens?

misconceptions.misconception: A business process is the software that runs it.
misconceptions.correction: The process is the flow of work and value; software is just a tool that executes part of it. The same process can run on paper or in an ERP.
Most risk lives at handoffs between steps and between departments — that's where errors and fraud slip through.

diagramNeeds.why: A left-to-right Procure-to-Pay flow makes inputs, activities, outputs, handoffs, and control points visible at a glance — impossible to convey as well in prose.

labIntel.why: Learners map a simple P2P or O2C flow for the recurring manufacturing example and mark where a control belongs. Hands-on system work is premature; the goal is the mental model.

instructions: Carry forward the SAME manufacturing example from Lesson 1.1.
Teach the business flow before mentioning any system or ERP.
Introduce 'control point' here but do NOT teach control types yet — that is Lesson 1.4.
Introduce the term Segregation of Duties (SoD) and define it; it will be reinforced repeatedly later.
Define every acronym (P2P, O2C, R2R, SoD) at first use.
Reinforce Lesson 1.1's value-creation idea: a process is how value actually gets created.

enrichment.mentalModel: Value is created by transactions flowing through a process; risk and controls live at the steps and especially the handoffs along that flow.

inScope: What a control point is and where it sits
Introducing the term Segregation of Duties
deferredToFuture: coso.v1.foundations.internal-controls teaches control types at those points
risk.v1.foundations.enterprise-risk teaches how to weigh what could go wrong
audit-evidence.v1.testing.test-of-design teaches how to test the control point

order: Define process with the factory example
Trace one purchase from request to payment
Show that a control point is just a place where we check something
Name segregation of duties at the approval/payment handoff
teachingStrategy.whyThisSequence: Tracing a concrete transaction first gives the learner something to point at; abstractions (control point, SoD) are then attached to a flow they can already picture, which is far stickier than defining terms cold.
analogyPoints: Process as an assembly line; handoffs as the moments a part passes between workers
Segregation of duties as 'the person who orders the parts can't also sign the cheque'
mandatoryDiagramsAt: The Procure-to-Pay process-flow diagram is mandatory when tracing the transaction

industryContext.scenario: Procure-to-Pay for raw materials: a planner raises a purchase order, receiving confirms delivery, Finance pays the invoice — three departments, two risky handoffs.
Order-to-Cash for patient billing, where a missed handoff between treatment coding and billing causes both revenue loss and compliance exposure.

auditContext.internalAudit: Internal Audit runs process walkthroughs to confirm the flow really works the way management describes before testing any control.
auditContext.externalAudit: External auditors scope financially significant processes (P2P, O2C, R2R) because that's where misstatement risk concentrates.
auditContext.compliance: Compliance checks that regulated steps (approvals, data handling) actually exist in the flow.
auditContext.executive: Executives care that processes are efficient and reliable enough to deliver value predictably.

vocabAdvanced: process risk and control matrix (RCM, taught later)

interviewAnswers.averageAnswer: 'Procure-to-Pay is when you buy something and pay for it.' — technically true, no grasp of steps, owners, or risk.
interviewAnswers.exceptionalAnswer: 'P2P flows from purchase requisition through approval, receipt, and three-way match to payment. The riskiest points are the approval and payment handoffs, which is why we segregate who can order from who can pay — and that's exactly where I'd expect to test a control.'

diagramDetail.learningObjective: Make the end-to-end transaction flow and its handoffs concrete so the learner can later point to exactly where a control belongs.
